\[
E(x) = \frac{1}{2 \sigma_n^2} \lVert h * x - g \rVert^2 + \frac{\lambda}{2}\, x^T \big(x - D(x)\big),
\qquad
x_{k+1} = \mathcal{F}^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\overline{H}\, \mathcal{F} g + \lambda \sigma_n^2\, \mathcal{F} D(x_k)}{\lvert H \rvert^2 + \lambda \sigma_n^2}\right),
\qquad
\lambda = 0.02,\ \sigma_n = 5
\]

The formula shows the default parameter values.

where

- \(g\): The blurred image extended with the border mode
- \(H\): The Fourier transform of the PSF
- \(D\): The denoiser, run with the denoiser sigma
- \(\sigma_n\): The noise sigma of the photo
- \(\lambda\): The weight of the denoiser penalty

Romano, Elad and Milanfar built a prior from a denoiser D. The penalty x^T (x - D(x)) is small when the image is close to what the denoiser would make of it. It is also small when the leftover x - D(x) does not line up with the image. Some denoisers change smoothly with the image and have a symmetric Jacobian. For them, the gradient of the penalty is lambda (x - D(x)). Setting the gradient of E to 0 gives (H^T H / sigma_n^2 + lambda) x = H^T g / sigma_n^2 + lambda D(x). The fixed-point method holds D(x) at the last estimate and solves this linear system exactly with the FFT. H is the transform of the PSF. Common denoisers only roughly meet the conditions, so the energy is a guide rather than a guarantee. The first estimate is the photo.
